title: Scarcity of skilled digital talent constrains SME and startup growth
description: Businesses trying to adopt modern software tools or build tech products report a shortage of workers skilled in areas like data analytics, digital marketing, and software development, forcing many to either train staff from scratch or operate without these capabilities altogether.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified
source: general knowledge / Nepal startup ecosystem coverage

title: Weak digital payment integration limits SME e-commerce potential
description: Even SMEs that want to sell online often cannot easily integrate reliable digital payment processing into their operations, given the fragmented state of Nepal's digital payment infrastructure and the cost and complexity of connecting to available payment gateways.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Manual, paper-based inventory and billing remain the norm for small retailers
description: Small shops and wholesalers across Nepal continue to track stock and sales using handwritten ledgers rather than digital systems, making it difficult to identify theft or spoilage losses, forecast restocking needs, or produce the transaction records formal lenders require for loan applications.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Cumbersome business registration and licensing discourage formalization
description: Cumbersome and sometimes inconsistently applied business registration, trademark, and licensing procedures add friction for entrepreneurs trying to formalize a venture, in some cases making it simpler to continue operating informally than to bear the cost and complexity of full legal registration.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Workplace sexual harassment persists despite a 2015 protection law
description: Nepal's Sexual Harassment at the Workplace (Elimination) Act of 2015 provides a legal framework against workplace harassment, but implementation remains weak, awareness of the law is limited even among employers, and many victims stay silent out of fear of retaliation, job loss, or social stigma.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified precisely (described as a 'serious challenge' in ILO analysis)

title: Technology-facilitated gender-based violence is a fast-growing threat
description: The rapid spread of social media and digital platforms has created new channels for harassment, stalking, and abuse targeting women and girls in Nepal, a form of violence that existing legal and law-enforcement frameworks are not yet well equipped to address.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Cross-border human trafficking of women and girls remains widespread
description: An estimated tens of women and girls are trafficked from Nepal into India every day, frequently by relatives or people known to them, for forced labor, forced marriage, or sexual exploitation, enabled by the long, largely open Nepal-India border and continuing rural poverty.
severity_or_scale: At least 54 women/girls trafficked into India daily, per National Human Rights Commission estimates

title: Persons with disabilities face pervasive infrastructure and attitude barriers
description: Inaccessible buildings, transportation, and public spaces, combined with negative social attitudes rooted in traditional beliefs about disability, exclude many disabled Nepalis from education, employment, and civic participation, with disaster-preparedness systems also often failing to account for their needs.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified
source: National Federation of the Disabled Nepal - https://www.nfdn.org.np/projects/accessibility-for-inclusion/

title: Children with disabilities face compounded barriers to education
description: Inaccessible school buildings and transportation, a shortage of teachers trained in inclusive education, and social stigma combine to keep many children with disabilities out of school entirely or push them into inadequate, unsupported learning environments.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified
source: general knowledge / disability education barriers research

title: Misinformation spreads faster than fact-checking capacity on social media
description: With media literacy still low, the great majority of Nepali internet users encounter misinformation regularly online, and young people in particular often consume and share content without the tools to verify its accuracy, accelerating the spread of false information faster than journalists or platforms can correct it.
severity_or_scale: A 2021 study found roughly 9 out of 10 Nepalis regularly receive misinformation online

title: Nepal has no national policy to counter disinformation
description: Despite widely acknowledged harm from fake news and disinformation campaigns, Nepal still lacks a coordinated national policy or regulatory framework specifically designed to counter the problem, leaving individual state bodies to introduce piecemeal, inconsistent responses.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Rural populations remain excluded from reliable news and information
description: With roughly two-thirds of Nepal's population living in rural areas but reliable independent journalism concentrated in Kathmandu and other urban centers, rural residents disproportionately rely on social media and word-of-mouth for news, making them more exposed to unchecked misinformation.
severity_or_scale: Nearly two-thirds of Nepal's population is rural and largely excluded from reliable news sources

title: Child marriage persists among poor, rural, marginalized-caste families
description: Despite a declining overall rate, child marriage remains common in poor rural communities where daughters are sometimes married early to reduce dowry costs or household economic burden, compounded by caste-based and gender-based discrimination that limits girls' other life options.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified precisely (described as still 'common' among poor rural families)

title: Child labor, including hidden child domestic work, remains widespread
description: Over a million Nepali children are engaged in child labor, mostly in agriculture, but a particularly hidden and normalized form involves children from poor rural families working as live-in domestic help in urban households, often facing long hours, isolation, and hazardous conditions with little oversight.
severity_or_scale: 1.1 million children in child labor nationally

title: Elderly Nepalis increasingly lack family caregivers due to migration
description: As working-age adults migrate abroad or to cities for work, a growing share of elderly Nepalis, especially women, are left without a co-resident caregiver, experiencing measurable increases in physical and emotional hardship, with no comprehensive national elder-care system to fill the gap.
severity_or_scale: 54.5% of surveyed elderly with migrant children reported physical problems linked to being left behind; 78.8% reported emotional problems

title: Most elderly Nepalis have no pension and must keep working
description: Because formal pension and social security coverage is limited, particularly for those who spent their working lives in agriculture or the informal sector, over half of older Nepalis remain economically active well into old age out of necessity rather than choice.
severity_or_scale: Over half of older Nepalis remain engaged in economic activity, mostly agriculture and self-employment

title: Dalit and marginalized-caste communities face persistent discrimination
description: Despite legal prohibitions on caste-based discrimination, Dalit and other marginalized communities continue to face unequal access to services, employment, and social inclusion, a disparity visible even in areas like internet access where higher-caste households are markedly more connected than Dalit households.
severity_or_scale: 37% of higher-caste households have internet access vs 21% of Dalit households

title: Justice system access is especially difficult for marginalized groups
description: Beyond the general court backlog, persons with disabilities, women, and other marginalized groups face additional structural barriers, including inaccessible court buildings and lack of interpreters or support services, that make it even harder for them to pursue legal remedies for rights violations.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified
source: National Federation of the Disabled Nepal - https://www.nfdn.org.np/external-resources/systemic-barriers-deny-justice-to-nepals-persons-with-disabilities/

title: Domestic violence and intimate partner abuse remain widely underreported
description: Social stigma, financial dependence, and fear of family or community backlash keep many cases of domestic and intimate-partner violence in Nepal from ever being reported to authorities, meaning official statistics likely substantially undercount the true scale of the problem.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified
source: general knowledge / Nepal gender-based violence literature

title: Cooperative embezzlement wiped out life savings of small depositors
description: A parliamentary investigation found roughly Rs 87.88 billion embezzled across 40 cooperatives, with over 500 savings and credit cooperatives nationwide unable to return depositors' money. Politically-connected operators (including a former home minister and a former mayor) allegedly diverted deposits into personal media companies, real estate, and unrelated businesses. Ordinary depositors, many of them retirees and small savers who trusted cooperatives over banks for better interest rates, have been left with no reliable recovery path years after the fraud surfaced.
severity_or_scale: ~76,000 depositors owed ~Rs46 billion at officially 'troubled' cooperatives; Rs87.88bn total embezzlement estimate from the parliamentary probe

title: Cooperative refund process discriminates against large depositors
description: The government's Problematic Cooperative Management Committee is prioritizing refunds only up to Rs 500,000 per depositor and only for cooperatives formally declared 'troubled,' leaving depositors with larger sums, or accounts at collapsed-but-unlisted cooperatives, with no defined path to recovery. Victims have staged repeated protests in Kathmandu since 2022 accusing the state of picking winners among fraud victims rather than resolving the sector systematically.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified beyond above figures; protest movement ongoing since 2022

title: No deposit insurance or resolution framework for failed cooperatives
description: Unlike commercial banks, Nepal's savings and credit cooperatives operate largely outside any functioning deposit-insurance or orderly-resolution regime, so when a cooperative's management disappears with member funds there is no institutional backstop analogous to bank deposit insurance. This regulatory gap let hundreds of cooperatives quietly become insolvent for years before the scale of the crisis became public.
severity_or_scale: 500+ cooperatives reported unable to return deposits

title: Cooperative operators divert member deposits into personal ventures undetected
description: Investigations into collapsed cooperatives such as Mahalaxmi/Gorkha Media and Image Savings and Credit Cooperative show operators funneling depositor money into media companies, real estate, and unrelated ventures rather than lending it back to members. Weak internal auditing and a toothless Department of Cooperatives allowed this diversion to continue for years before collapse, with no early-warning system catching the anomalies.
severity_or_scale: individual cases cited over Rs2 billion each (e.g. Image Cooperative ~Rs2.25 billion)

title: Cooperative regulator lacks capacity to supervise tens of thousands of local cooperatives
description: Nepal has tens of thousands of registered cooperatives spread across all provinces, far outstripping the National Cooperative Regulatory Authority's inspection and audit capacity, which lets fraudulent operators run undetected for years. There is currently no regtech tool used at scale to flag anomalous lending or deposit patterns across the sector before a cooperative collapses.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Informal rotating-savings and dhukuti-style groups sit entirely outside fraud recourse
description: Alongside registered-but-poorly-supervised cooperatives, many Nepali communities also rely on wholly informal rotating savings/credit clubs (dhukuti-type groups) that carry zero regulatory registration, so when an organizer absconds with pooled funds there is no legal entity or regulator to even file a complaint against. This sits one level further outside the formal system than the cooperatives already implicated in the national scandal and is essentially undocumented in official fraud statistics.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: eSewa-Khalti wallet-to-wallet transfer still not live despite tech readiness
description: Nepal Rastra Bank mandated interoperability between digital wallets in 2022, and eSewa says the switch (via FonePay/NCHL) is already technically interoperable, yet users still cannot directly transfer balance between eSewa and Khalti years later. The holdup is commercial: the two largest wallets haven't agreed on revenue-sharing and operational terms, and Khalti's ongoing merger with IME Pay has added further uncertainty over which merged entity a user would even be transacting with.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified; affects millions of active digital wallet users

title: Cross-border NepalPay QR for India/Bhutan stuck on commission disputes
description: Nepal Rastra Bank approved QR payments for Nepalis traveling to India and Bhutan, but rollout has been repeatedly delayed because banks and payment operators cannot agree on who bears the transaction commission and how much each side of the retail switch earns. Nepali travelers and small tourism/export businesses catering to Indian visitors are left without a functioning low-cost cross-border QR rail.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified; rollout delayed well past original 2024 target

title: Merchant settlement timing differs by wallet/bank, complicating SME cash flow
description: Small merchants accepting eSewa, Khalti, and FonePay QR codes face different settlement schedules (commonly T+1 for wallets, but dependent on the acquiring bank's own processing calendar for FonePay), making daily cash-flow reconciliation harder for shopkeepers with no accounting staff. No single unified settlement/reconciliation dashboard exists for a small vendor accepting multiple payment schemes at once.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Bulk-SMS spoofing lets fraudsters impersonate banks and wallets to steal OTPs
description: Nepal's Cyber Bureau has flagged a wave of SMS phishing where attackers compromise bulk-SMS provider accounts to send fake transaction alerts that land in the same message thread as genuine texts from Khalti or ConnectIPS, tricking victims into revealing OTPs or credentials. A May 2025 case saw Rs 3.48 million stolen from a single ConnectIPS account this way, with 13 people eventually charged months later.
severity_or_scale: Rs3.48 million lost in one documented 2025 case

title: Ride-hailing drivers have no legal minimum fare or labor protection
description: Nepal has no formal law regulating ride-hailing, so companies like Pathao, inDrive, Yango and Uber set commission and fare policy unilaterally; drivers say inDrive long-distance trips barely cover fuel while Pathao takes a 20% commission. Drivers staged a sit-in demanding a uniform minimum base fare of Rs 25/km, which Pathao, Yango and Uber agreed to but inDrive refused, and no binding agreement has been reached because no regulator exists to enforce one.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified; nationwide driver protests recurring 2024-2026

title: Ride-hailing operates in legal limbo with no government guidelines
description: Years after platforms like Pathao and inDrive launched, the government still hasn't issued promised regulations for digital mobility services, leaving companies formally unregistered as transport operators and drivers without clear legal status, insurance requirements, or dispute-resolution channels. Police have periodically cracked down on 'offline' ride-hailing (drivers arranging trips outside the app to dodge commissions) precisely because the legal category for the industry doesn't exist yet.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Delivery and ride-hailing gig workers fall outside Nepal's labor law
description: Nepal's Labour Act does not clearly classify app-based delivery riders and drivers as employees, so platforms aren't obligated to provide the accident insurance, minimum wage, or social-security contributions formal-sector workers receive. Legal commentators describe this rapidly growing workforce as 'legally invisible,' with no statutory recourse if injured on the job or terminated without cause.
severity_or_scale: gig economy reported ~67% growth; workforce size not officially quantified

title: Festival-season fare gouging on ride-hailing apps goes unpunished
description: During peak periods like Tihar, passengers report being charged extreme surge fares (e.g., Rs 2,700 for a short Naya Thimi-to-Kapan trip) with no cap or regulatory penalty, alongside complaints of rude drivers and unexplained delays. Because no consumer-protection body actively monitors ride-hailing pricing, there is no channel for passengers to dispute or get refunded for these spikes.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Multiple concurrent MFI loans trap rural women's groups in debt spirals
description: A Nepal Rastra Bank survey found 37% of microfinance borrowers held loans from at least two MFIs simultaneously, often because women's group-lending members take a new loan from a second institution just to service the first. This 'multiple banking' behavior is driven by intense MFI competition for the same rural client base rather than any real assessment of borrowers' repayment capacity.
severity_or_scale: 37% of borrowers had loans from 2+ MFIs per 2017 NRB survey

title: Microfinance mission drift shifts from poverty relief to high-interest lending
description: What began as subsidized, socially-oriented microcredit for poor women has drifted toward a profit-driven model with higher effective interest rates and aggressive loan-officer targets, leaving many women's groups with debt burdens disproportionate to their enterprise income. No shared, cross-institution credit check is consistently enforced at the group-lending level to prevent over-lending to the same household.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Supreme Court backlog leaves cases pending for nearly two decades
description: Nearly 27,000 cases remain sub judice at Nepal's Supreme Court, some pending for almost twenty years, with 1,258 cases stuck for more than five years. Litigants in property, family, or criminal appeals face years of uncertainty and repeated court appearances with no digital case-tracking transparency into where their file actually sits in the queue.
severity_or_scale: ~27,000 pending cases at Supreme Court; 1,258 pending 5+ years

title: Judicial vacancies across all court tiers slow case clearance nationwide
description: The constitution allows 20 Supreme Court judges but only 14 are serving, with 39 vacant seats at district courts and 55 at high courts, directly cutting the system's hearing capacity. Combined with district courts alone holding over 107,000 pending cases, the vacancy problem compounds delays that already stretch for years for ordinary litigants.
severity_or_scale: 20 authorized/14 serving Supreme Court judges; 107,130 pending district-court cases

title: No e-filing or case-tracking system lets court files get lost or delayed
description: Part of Nepal's backlog stems from court files simply failing to arrive on time between benches and registries, and from cases with numerous litigants/advocates being repeatedly rescheduled. No robust nationwide e-filing or case-status system lets litigants or lawyers check progress remotely instead of visiting court in person.
severity_or_scale: 160,549 disputes unresolved out of 357,023 pending across all tiers in one recent snapshot

title: Social stigma keeps most gender-based violence unreported despite legal reforms
description: Despite Nepal passing multiple gender-responsive laws since 2015, formal help-seeking for GBV remains low because community norms discourage women from reporting and sanction those who do, per a mixed-methods baseline study of security and justice services. Nearly a third of Nepali women report having experienced physical or sexual violence in their lifetime, yet the gap between incidence and formal case filing remains wide.
severity_or_scale: ~33% of women report lifetime physical/sexual violence (2022 Demographic and Health Survey)

title: Low prosecution rates for reported GBV cases due to corruption and delay
description: Even when women report abuse, corruption, insufficiently trained personnel, and lengthy legal proceedings keep prosecution rates low, and marginalized women (Dalit, Indigenous, Madhesi, Muslim, disabled) face compounded barriers to justice. There is no dedicated, well-resourced fast-track case-management system connecting police, one-stop crisis centers, and courts specifically for GBV survivors.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: No unified case-tracking links police, health, and legal aid for GBV survivors
description: UNFPA's Nepal work on tracking GBV cases documents how survivors must navigate separate, disconnected police, health, and judicial systems with no shared case ID or status visibility, making it easy for cases to stall or for survivors to give up mid-process. Field organizations rely on manual, paper-based tracking that varies district to district.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Zero of Kathmandu's audited public transport sites are disability-accessible
description: An accessibility audit of 150 public infrastructure sites in Kathmandu found that none of the 13 transportation-sector sites were adequately accessible for people with disabilities. Visually impaired and wheelchair-using passengers report buses that don't fully stop, rushed boarding, and no tactile or audio cues at stops.
severity_or_scale: 0 of 13 audited transport sites adequately accessible

title: No technical standard exists for disability-accessible roads or pavements
description: Unlike markets with mandated tactile paving and curb-cut specifications, Nepal has no established standard for disability-friendly pavements, ramps, or bus-stop heights, so even new infrastructure projects are inconsistently accessible. This leaves compliance with the 2017 Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act essentially unenforceable at the construction stage.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Disability rights law exists on paper but enforcement mechanisms are absent
description: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2017 mandates accessible public buildings, transport and services, but implementation remains weak, with no penalty regime that consistently forces builders, bus operators or ministries to comply. Advocacy groups describe most 'accessible' retrofits as symbolic rather than functional.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Kathmandu Valley's informal settlements quadrupled since the 1980s with no tenure security
description: Squatter communities in Kathmandu Valley grew from 17 in 1985 to roughly 65 today, housing over 28,000 people, most without formal land tenure, water, or sanitation connections. New rural migrants keep clustering in shrinking open spaces and environmentally sensitive riverbank areas because no affordable formal housing alternative exists near job centers.
severity_or_scale: ~28,000 people across 65 informal settlements in Kathmandu Valley

title: 2026 riverbank evictions left thousands in temporary shelters with inadequate compensation
description: Since April 2026 the government has demolished riverbank informal settlements across Kathmandu Valley, moving roughly 2,600 displaced people through Dasharath Stadium into temporary holding centers, prompting a Supreme Court order demanding due process and basic services. Displaced families say the Rs 15,000 monthly rental allowance offered doesn't cover actual Kathmandu Valley rents of Rs 25,000-30,000 for even a modest flat.
severity_or_scale: ~2,600 people displaced; rental-allowance gap of roughly Rs10,000-15,000/month

title: No affordable-housing finance product serves informal-sector urban migrants
description: Urban migrants working informally (construction, domestic work, small trade) generally cannot access mortgage products designed around salaried, documented income, pushing them toward informal settlements or overcrowded rental rooms near job centers. No government or private housing-finance scheme specifically targets this segment with flexible income verification.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Hill and mountain villages are emptying into 'ghost villages' as young people leave
description: Studies estimate over 60% of highland rural settlements could be abandoned within 15 years as agriculture becomes unviable on small, eroded, fragmented hill plots; in Kuruletenupa only 5 of 50 houses remain occupied, and districts like Dhankuta, Ramechhap, Khotang, Manang, Bhojpur and Tehrathum saw the fastest population loss in the latest census decade. Remaining residents are disproportionately elderly, straining already-thin local health and care services.
severity_or_scale: up to 60%+ of highland settlements projected abandoned within 15 years per one watershed study

title: Kathmandu Metro absorbs 35% of all internal migrants, overwhelming municipal services
description: Thirty-five percent of all rural-to-urban migrants nationally end up in Kathmandu Metropolitan City alone, where migrants now make up 57% of the population, driving unplanned sprawl and school/health overcrowding faster than infrastructure can be built. No secondary-city incentive program has meaningfully redirected migration away from the Valley.
severity_or_scale: 35% of national rural-urban migrants concentrate in KMC; migrants = 57% of KMC population

title: Rural internet penetration is less than a quarter of urban penetration
description: Only about 17.4% of rural Nepali households have internet access compared to over 79% of urban households, and the gap is starkest by province — Kathmandu Valley sits at 79.3% penetration versus Karnali Province at just 14%. Mountainous terrain makes fiber and tower rollout costly, and operators generally only plan expansion where 100-200+ potential subscribers exist in one area.
severity_or_scale: 17.4% rural vs 79%+ urban household internet access; Karnali at 14%

title: Unreliable power undermines rural connectivity even where towers exist
description: In many mountain districts, cell towers and fiber nodes exist on paper but deliver unstable service because of unreliable grid electricity and the high cost of running backup generators or solar at remote sites. Official 'coverage' statistics consequently overstate the actually-usable connectivity rural users experience day to day.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Commercially-driven telecom rollout leaves low-demand remote wards permanently unserved
description: Telecom operators generally only extend networks to areas expected to yield 100-200 subscribers, meaning sparsely populated mountain wards may never receive commercial investment absent a dedicated rural connectivity fund reaching that last mile. Community-driven projects like Nepal Wireless have filled small gaps but cover only a fraction of underserved wards.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: EV battery e-waste has no regulated collection or recycling system
description: Nepal's EV imports surged to 44,509 vehicles in FY2024/25, but the country has no laws, infrastructure, or recycling systems for the lithium-ion batteries and electronic components these vehicles will eventually discard, creating a looming toxic-waste problem with zero current collection pathway. The same regulatory gap applies to the broader surge in imported consumer electronics generally.
severity_or_scale: 44,509 EVs imported in FY2024/25

title: 450+ tonnes of plastic waste generated daily with no source segregation
description: Nepal generates over 450 metric tonnes of plastic waste daily, much of it ending up in rivers, open dumps, or landfills because households and businesses aren't required or equipped to segregate waste at the point of generation. Municipal plastic-bag bans exist on paper in several cities but enforcement is weak, and no deposit-return or extended-producer-responsibility system operates at scale.
severity_or_scale: 450+ metric tonnes/day of plastic waste

title: Bancharedanda landfill protests repeatedly halt waste collection valley-wide
description: Locals near the Bancharedanda landfill on the Nuwakot-Dhading border have blocked waste trucks multiple times since 2022 over unfulfilled promises (Guthi land registration, relocation of the worst-affected households, road upgrades, and scientific waste segregation), each time paralyzing garbage collection across Kathmandu Valley for days. Across this site and its predecessor Sisdol, spanning 18 years, authorities have signed 175 agreements with locals, essentially none of which have been implemented.
severity_or_scale: 175 unimplemented agreements over 18 years; each protest halts collection valley-wide

title: Landfill leachate contaminates streams and farmland around Bancharedanda
description: Because biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste isn't separated before reaching the landfill, leachate has overflowed containment dams and flowed into nearby streams, causing crop-yield loss, livestock disease, and respiratory/skin illness among surrounding villagers. Affected households report disrupted schooling from the stench, with no scientific lining or leachate-treatment upgrade delivered despite two decades of complaints.
severity_or_scale: documented health/agricultural harm ongoing for roughly 20 years; scale not separately quantified

title: No source-segregation infrastructure exists across most municipalities
description: Local governments across Nepal cite critical shortages of budget, trucks, and landfill capacity, and lack of waste segregation at the source is repeatedly identified as the single biggest complication for recycling. Without segregated collection bins or schedules, informal waste pickers end up doing manual, hazardous sorting directly at dumpsites instead.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Municipal fleets lack garbage trucks and engineered landfill capacity to scale collection
description: Outside Kathmandu Valley, many municipalities report basic shortages of garbage trucks and engineered disposal sites, forcing open burning, riverside dumping, or irregular collection schedules on a limited local revenue base. This is a distinct infrastructure gap from the segregation/recycling problem — it's simply insufficient fleet and disposal-site capacity that small municipalities cannot self-fund.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Unregulated construction dust is a bigger PM10 source than vehicles in Kathmandu
description: Studies attribute 53% of Kathmandu Valley's PM10 emissions to construction activity, more than the 30% attributed to transport, yet dust-suppression requirements (site netting, water spraying, covered material transport) are rarely enforced at construction sites. This makes construction dust an under-addressed pollution source relative to the policy attention vehicles and brick kilns receive.
severity_or_scale: construction = 53% of PM10 vs transport at 30%

title: 110 brick kilns in the Valley contribute a third of dust pollution with weak emissions control
description: As of 2017, 110 brick kilns operated in Kathmandu Valley (63 in Bhaktapur alone), contributing roughly a third of the Valley's dust pollution and exposing kiln workers directly to high particulate and sulfur-dioxide levels, with documented respiratory illness among workers. Cleaner zigzag-kiln technology exists but adoption remains partial due to cost and weak enforcement of emissions standards.
severity_or_scale: 110 kilns valley-wide; ~1/3 of Valley dust pollution attributed to the brick industry

title: Kathmandu's bowl topography traps seasonal pollution with no coordinated valley-wide response
description: Kathmandu's bowl-shaped geography means that without rain or wind (worst January-May and November-December), pollution from vehicles, kilns, construction, and open burning stays trapped over the city, regularly placing it among the world's most polluted capitals during these months. Authority over emissions sources is fragmented across many municipalities plus provincial and federal agencies, hampering any single enforceable clean-air plan.
severity_or_scale: Kathmandu ranked among the top 10 most polluted cities globally, April 2026

title: Overcrowded microbuses create a documented harassment risk for women commuters
description: About 18.8% of passengers perceive microbuses as unsafe, and overcrowding on these vehicles is specifically cited as enabling molestation, making public transport 'a space of vulnerability' for women according to World Bank research on gender and transport in Nepal. No women-only carriage, real-time reporting app, or in-vehicle monitoring operates at meaningful scale to address this.
severity_or_scale: 18.8% of passengers rate microbuses unsafe

title: Uncoordinated private bus operators mean no fixed schedules or reliable stops
description: Kathmandu's public transport runs through numerous independent private operators with no centralized schedule, so buses arrive at inconsistent intervals, GPS tracking (where it exists) is inaccurate, and vehicles stop wherever convenient — mid-intersection, near schools, or suddenly in traffic — rather than at designated stops. This raises both accident risk and commute-time unpredictability that no existing app reliably solves.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Ride-hailing hasn't solved Kathmandu's student commuting gap
description: Students struggling with unreliable, unsafe public buses have turned to ride-hailing apps, but fares are too expensive for daily commuting on a student budget, leaving many with no genuinely workable option between an unreliable Rs 20-30 bus and a Rs 300+ ride-share trip. No subsidized or pooled ride product currently bridges this specific price/reliability gap.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Right-of-way and forest-clearance disputes delay export-critical transmission lines
description: A major cross-border-enabling transmission project has been delayed by Right of Way disputes with private landowners and slow forest-clearance approvals, directly threatening Nepal's ability to deliver power under signed export agreements with India and Bangladesh. Each delay risks confidence in Nepal as a reliable power-trade partner even though domestic generation capacity itself is not the constraint.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified; project timeline pushed back by months

title: India's approval bottleneck blocks Nepal from expanding Bangladesh power exports
description: Even with a working tripartite Nepal-India-Bangladesh arrangement, India's Central Electricity Authority has withheld approval for an additional 20 MW of Nepal-to-Bangladesh exports over transmission-capacity concerns, and Nepal cannot export another 73.75 MW from three hydropower projects because India hasn't renewed those export approvals. This makes Nepal's power-export revenue hostage to a third country's unilateral regulatory timeline.
severity_or_scale: 20 MW blocked; 73.75 MW in unrenewed export approvals

title: Monsoon hydropower surplus gets curtailed instead of powering domestic industry
description: During monsoon, Nepal's generation (installed capacity ~4,300 MW) exceeds roughly 3,400 MW of combined domestic-plus-export demand, forcing the Nepal Electricity Authority to order developers to curtail output — nearly 900 MW can go unabsorbed at peak river flow — even as industries still burn imported diesel/LPG for processes that could run on this wasted electricity. No large-scale industrial demand (green hydrogen, cold storage, EV charging hubs, data centers) has been built fast enough to absorb the seasonal surplus.
severity_or_scale: up to ~900 MW unabsorbed during monsoon peaks

title: Pancheshwar cross-border mega-hydropower project stalled for 30 years
description: Nepal and India agreed to jointly build the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project three decades ago, but construction still hasn't begun because the two governments cannot agree on the detailed project report — illustrating how bilateral political and technical deadlock, not financing or technology, is the binding constraint on some of Nepal's largest potential hydropower assets.
severity_or_scale: 30 years stalled with no construction start

title: Annual fertilizer shortage forces farmers to buy at up to 5x price on the black market
description: Nepal imports nearly all its urea, DAP and potash, mostly through Indian ports and border customs where procedural bottlenecks, truck shortages, and political strikes routinely delay shipments right as planting season starts. The resulting shortage forces farmers to either shrink cultivated area or pay black-market prices reported as high as five times the official rate, a pattern that has repeated almost every planting season for years.
severity_or_scale: farmers report paying up to 5x the official price on the black market

title: Vegetable losses of up to 41% occur between farm and retail due to poor logistics
description: A wholesale-market loss study found post-harvest losses reaching 41% for cauliflower and 34% for cabbage at the retailer level, driven by improper packaging, no field-heat removal before shipping, poor grading/sorting, and inadequate transport — far above losses at the farm/collection-center stage. Cold-storage pilots (e.g. solar-powered units in Dolakha) cut total potato loss to 4.38% versus 13.04% for in-house storage, showing the fix is proven but not scaled.
severity_or_scale: up to 41% retail-level loss for cauliflower; cold storage cuts potato loss from ~13% to ~4.4%

title: Dairy processors owe farmers billions in unpaid milk dues
description: Milk-processing companies owed roughly Rs 6 billion nationwide to farmers at one point, with Chitwan farmers alone awaiting Rs 520 million, triggering sustained protests by the National Peasants' Coalition against 'one-sided' payment agreements they weren't party to negotiating. Farmers say cooperatives buy milk at Rs 45-50/liter and resell at Rs 65/liter while consumers pay up to Rs 80/liter, showing most margin is captured by intermediaries rather than producers.
severity_or_scale: ~Rs6 billion owed nationwide to milk producers (2024)

title: 500,000-600,000 liters of milk wasted daily for lack of market despite farmer distress
description: Nepal produces about 7.1 million liters of milk daily across roughly 300,000 producing households, yet 500,000-600,000 liters are wasted daily for lack of a functioning market or processing channel, even as the state-owned Dairy Development Corporation sits on unsold stockpiles of butter and powdered milk. This oversupply-and-waste paradox coexists with farmers simultaneously complaining of unpaid dues, pointing to a broken distribution/processing-capacity matching problem rather than genuine oversupply.
severity_or_scale: 500,000-600,000 liters/day wasted; DDC holding 600 tonnes butter and 500 tonnes powdered milk in stockpile

title: Crop insurance penetration is around 1%, far below livestock/fish insurance uptake
description: Nepal's crop-specific agricultural insurance penetration sits near 1% (versus a broader 3-4.4% counting livestock and fish), hampered by complex documentation, slow or disputed claim settlement, low farmer awareness, and damage assessments that are difficult to execute in remote terrain. Indemnity-based products currently on the market suit wealthier farmers better than the smallholders who most need climate-risk protection.
severity_or_scale: ~1% crop insurance penetration; ~4.4% overall agri-insurance participation after 10 years of the program

title: 73% of villages lack government veterinary services despite hundreds of registered vets
description: Nearly 73% of Nepali villages remain without government-supported veterinary services even though 698 veterinarians are registered nationally, indicating a severe geographic maldistribution rather than an absolute shortage of trained professionals. Most of the 5,000+ village animal health workers who do reach rural areas report being technically under-equipped and underutilized by local farmers.
severity_or_scale: 73% of villages without government vet services; 698 registered vets nationally

title: Inadequate cold-chain infrastructure undermines livestock vaccine delivery
description: Farmers report significant economic losses from delayed detection and treatment of animal disease, worsened by insufficient cold-chain infrastructure for vaccine storage and a shortage of diagnostic equipment and trained lab technicians in rural service centers. Transboundary diseases like foot-and-mouth disease, PPR, and lumpy skin disease consequently spread faster and cause larger economic losses than they would with functioning surveillance and vaccine logistics.
severity_or_scale: described as 'millions of dollars' in recent-year losses generally; not precisely quantified

title: Shortage of AI technicians and ultrasound specialists limits herd productivity
description: A shortage of trained human resources — skilled ultrasound technicians, artificial-insemination experts, and lab technicians — combined with insufficient diagnostic facilities is limiting the capacity of livestock service centers to help farmers improve breeding outcomes and productivity. This technical-skills gap is distinct from general vet shortages and specifically blocks dairy/livestock productivity gains that development programs are trying to unlock.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Post-earthquake resettlement sites failed because they ignored farmland and livelihood needs
description: After the 2015 earthquake, roughly 500 settlements were classified high-risk (CAT I) and needed relocation, but planned sites like Tiru in Rasuwa failed for most families because moving there meant losing farmland with no alternative livelihood offered, so people drifted back to floodplain land along the Trishuli River. A community of 250 households that resettled this way was later swept away entirely in floods, and survivors report the same failure pattern repeating at the next relocation attempt (Tallopahire, half of which was also destroyed).
severity_or_scale: ~500 settlements classified high-risk (CAT I) post-2015 earthquake; 250-household community later swept away in floods

title: No operational glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) early-warning system exists
description: Nepal currently has no functioning GLOF early-warning system, and existing flood/landslide alerts don't extend to glacial-lake monitoring at all, despite GLOFs and landslide-dam-burst floods (like the Melamchi disaster) being able to reach downstream villages within minutes of triggering. Watershed-level adaptation and monitoring investment has lacked sustainable funding, per ICIMOD analysis.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified; flood can reach a valley floor within minutes of the trigger event in some configurations

title: 2015 earthquake housing-grant tranche system was misaligned with the actual rebuild pace
description: The National Reconstruction Authority disbursed private housing grants in tranches tied to construction milestones, but by the January 2018 deadline only 204,993 of 669,542 eligible households had received their second tranche, and many families had already rebuilt without NRA-mandated seismic features before receiving the first payment, disqualifying them from further support. The NRA itself wasn't established until eight months after the earthquake, baking in delay from the start.
severity_or_scale: 204,993 of 669,542 households had received the second tranche by the January 2018 deadline

title: 2026 Bhotekoshi flood survivors remain in relocation limbo
description: Communities displaced by the 2026 Bhotekoshi flood are still waiting for the government to decide on and implement relocation options months after the disaster, echoing the same post-2015-earthquake pattern where resettlement planning drags on long enough that people return to at-risk land out of necessity. No standing, pre-funded rapid-resettlement protocol exists that would let a relocation decision and livelihood plan happen within weeks rather than months or years.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Cybercrime cases hit roughly 52/day with youth dominating both victims and perpetrators
description: Nepal recorded 18,926 cybercrime cases in FY2024-25, averaging 52 per day, with 70% of cyber-fraud suspects aged 19-30 — suggesting the same digitally-fluent youth cohort struggling to find formal jobs is also disproportionately represented in fraud rings. Nepal Police's Cyber Bureau capacity has not scaled proportionally with this case growth.
severity_or_scale: 18,926 cases in FY2024-25 (~52/day); 70% of suspects aged 19-30

title: No reimbursement guarantee exists for phishing/OTP-fraud victims of banks or wallets
description: Unlike markets with mandated fraud-liability-shift rules, Nepali banking and wallet customers who lose money to phishing generally have no guaranteed reimbursement path — recovery depends on catching and prosecuting the fraudster, a slow process, as shown by the 13-defendant ConnectIPS case that took months to result in charges after a Rs 3.48 million theft. This leaves individual consumers bearing nearly all fraud risk despite banks controlling the security infrastructure.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified nationally

title: Pashmina exports fell fourfold in five years amid quality and counterfeit concerns
description: Nepal's pashmina exports dropped to roughly Rs 42 million in the most recent fiscal year reported, a fourfold decline over five years, driven partly by quality concerns in European markets and competition from mass-produced synthetic 'pashmina' undercutting genuine hand-woven product on price. Nepal currently captures only 0.5-1% of global demand in categories like pashmina despite having the artisanal heritage to command a premium.
severity_or_scale: pashmina exports down to ~Rs42 million, a 4x decline over 5 years; 0.5-1% global market share

title: Artisans remain dependent on middlemen with no direct export market access
description: Handicraft and pashmina artisans typically lack direct contact with either raw-material sources or end buyers, dealing instead through layers of middlemen who capture most of the margin, described by sector analysts as an 'endless circle of exploitation.' Poor rural infrastructure (unreliable power, bad roads) further limits artisans' ability to complete orders on time or transport goods to export hubs themselves.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Younger generation's declining interest threatens transmission of traditional craft skills
description: Sector reporting notes younger Nepalis are increasingly uninterested in learning traditional weaving, metalwork, and pashmina-making skills, partly because these trades offer inconsistent income compared to migration or urban service jobs, risking a generational skills gap in crafts that make up a meaningful heritage export category. No structured apprenticeship-to-income pipeline currently bridges this gap at scale.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Foreign investment approval requires sequential FITTA + DOI + OCR steps taking 2-4 months
description: A foreign investor or Nepali startup seeking foreign capital must first get approval under FITTA 2075, then wait for Department of Industry sign-off, before the Office of the Company Registrar will even process incorporation — a strictly sequential, multi-agency process typically taking 2-4 months, with common rejection triggers being name inconsistencies between the MOA and application, missing ID numbers, or unsigned documents. This timeline and rejection risk deters smaller international investors or accelerator-backed startups needing to close funding quickly.
severity_or_scale: 2-4 months typical timeline; minimum FDI threshold USD 20,000/investor

title: Nepali freelancers and SaaS founders can't use PayPal, forcing reliance on workaround rails
description: PayPal remains officially unavailable for Nepali users due to NRB foreign-exchange and payment-gateway rules, so freelancers and small software/service exporters on Upwork, Fiverr, or direct international contracts must route payments through Payoneer, Wise, or informal channels, often paying more in fees and facing slower settlement than counterparts in markets where PayPal operates. This is a direct tax on Nepal's ability to compete for global remote-services income.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Limited domestic VC/angel capital pushes founders toward collateral-based bank debt
description: Beyond a small number of SEBON-registered venture funds and angel investors, most Nepali entrepreneurs must rely on bank loans requiring physical collateral (land/property) — a financing structure poorly suited to early-stage, asset-light startups with no revenue history. Government-backed innovation loan guarantees exist but are not yet widely used or well-known among founders.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Cryptocurrency ban blocks crypto-native business models and payment rails
description: Nepal Rastra Bank has banned cryptocurrency trading and use since 2021, closing off an entire category of fintech business models (crypto exchanges, stablecoin remittance products, tokenized assets) that founders elsewhere use to route around exactly the cross-border payment friction Nepali freelancers and SMEs face. This leaves a policy-created gap between what's technically possible for cross-border settlement and what's legally permitted.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Periodic luxury-import bans create inventory planning risk for import-dependent retailers
description: To defend depleting foreign-exchange reserves, Nepal has repeatedly banned imports of specific goods (large TVs, high-cc motorbikes, liquor, tobacco, certain electronics) with limited advance notice, leaving small importers and retailers who had already ordered stock or signed distribution agreements exposed to sudden compliance risk and unsellable inventory. No hedging mechanism or advance-notice protocol lets SMEs adjust orders before a ban takes effect.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: SME foreign-currency import limits constrain working capital for growing businesses
description: Business import forex limits were raised to USD 100,000 from USD 60,000, but this remains a hard ceiling that can constrain a growing SME's ability to place larger, more cost-efficient bulk orders from overseas suppliers, especially compared to larger competitors with separate LC arrangements. Smaller import-reliant businesses (electronics, building materials, machinery parts) must structure purchases around this cap rather than around actual market opportunity.
severity_or_scale: current business goods-import forex limit: USD 100,000

title: Remittance-dependent forex reserves create sudden, unplannable trade restrictions for SMEs
description: Because roughly a quarter of Nepal's GDP flows in through remittances, any slowdown in outbound labor migration or a spike in imports quickly threatens foreign-exchange reserves, which in turn triggers sudden central-bank measures like import bans or tightened LC requirements that businesses can't plan around in advance. Import-dependent SMEs have no forward-looking signal or hedging product to anticipate when the next forex-driven restriction might hit their specific product category.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: University graduates are three times more likely to be unemployed than the uneducated
description: Youth unemployment stood at 20.8% in 2024, but graduate unemployment specifically reached 26.1% — three times the rate among Nepalis with no formal education — indicating the credential itself isn't translating into job access, likely due to outdated curricula disconnected from actual employer needs. Over 60% of employers report difficulty finding candidates with the skills they need, while 45% of graduates end up working in fields unrelated to their degree.
severity_or_scale: 26.1% graduate unemployment vs 20.8% overall youth unemployment; 60% of employers report skill-gap hiring difficulty

title: 92% of employed Nepali youth work in the informal economy with no job security
description: Roughly 92% of employed young Nepalis are in informal employment — low wages, no contracts, no social security, and no clear promotion path — even when they hold degrees, because the formal private sector isn't creating enough structured jobs to absorb the annual graduate cohort. Government job programs (PMEP, Youth Vision 2025) exist but suffer from fragmentation and weak private-sector coordination.
severity_or_scale: 92% of employed youth in informal employment

title: Vocational (CTEVT) training pipeline isn't coordinated with actual private-sector hiring needs
description: Nepal's technical and vocational training system (CTEVT) trains students in specific trades, but sector reviews find limited coordination between what's taught and what private employers are actually hiring for, plus little performance monitoring of whether graduates get placed in relevant jobs at all. This leaves a structural mismatch even in the one part of the education system explicitly designed for job-readiness.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Guthi trust land is being encroached and privatized with unimplemented oversight
description: A 2005 government task force documented widespread encroachment of temple/Guthi land and disappearing sacred ponds, but its recommendations were never implemented; specific cases include roughly 15,262 sq. m of the Ram Mandir Guthi land at Devghatdham and heavy encroachment of Chandannath Bhairavnath Guthi land in Jumla via illegal roads and private construction. In some cases the very priests (mahants) entrusted to manage temple land have privately sold or transferred it, and misappropriation has caused some Guthis to stop functioning entirely, ending centuries-old rituals.
severity_or_scale: 15,262 sq.m. encroached at one documented site (Ram Mandir Guthi); 20-year-old task force report unimplemented

title: No functioning digital registry prevents systematic tracking of Guthi land boundaries
description: Because Guthi land records are scattered, paper-based, and not integrated with the national land-survey digitization effort, encroachment often goes undetected for years or decades until a task force or journalist investigation surfaces it — as happened in Janakpur, where a 20-year-old task force report on Guthi land was simply ignored. Systematic reclamation or protection is nearly impossible without a dedicated GIS-based Guthi land mapping tool.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Inconsistent land-parcel maps across old and digitized records fuel ownership disputes
description: As Nepal digitizes cadastral records, discrepancies between historical paper maps and newly digitized parcel boundaries are surfacing, and server outages at land offices periodically halt transactions entirely. Until parcel maps are reconciled with actual on-the-ground utilization and ownership documents rebuilt against corrected maps, land disputes rooted in minor historical survey errors will keep recurring and clogging courts.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Rising bank non-performing loans expose real-estate over-concentration and falsified reporting
description: The average NPL ratio across Nepali banks climbed from 3.66% to 4.42% between October 2023 and October 2024, with regulators and IMF auditors flagging excessive real-estate loan concentration as a specific driver, compounded by a land-use act change that froze certain land transactions. A parallel case saw Karnali Development Bank suspended by Nepal Rastra Bank after falsifying its NPL data, raising questions about how many other institutions' reported asset quality is unreliable.
severity_or_scale: NPL ratio rose from 3.66% to 4.42% (Oct 2023-Oct 2024)

title: Informal hundi remittance channel costs Nepal hundreds of millions in lost foreign currency
description: Hundi (hawala-style) transfers are illegal under Nepal's Foreign Exchange Regulation Act but persist because they're faster (hours vs. days) and roughly three times cheaper than formal remittance channels; a 2017 study estimated Nepal Rastra Bank misses out on about USD 384 million a year from South Korea alone through this single corridor. Hundi is also used to launder proceeds from gold smuggling and other illegal activity, and it starves the formal fintech remittance sector of transaction volume that legitimate apps could otherwise capture.
severity_or_scale: ~USD 384 million/year estimated lost via hundi from the South Korea corridor alone (2017 study)

title: VAT/tax compliance burden is disproportionately heavy for micro and small enterprises
description: Registered Nepali businesses must maintain detailed records, issue compliant invoices, file monthly returns, and undergo periodic audits regardless of size — a process research shows many small business owners find complex enough that perceived compliance cost can outweigh the benefit of formal registration altogether. This pushes many microenterprises to stay informal, shrinking the tax base and locking those businesses out of formal credit, government tenders, and B2B contracts that require tax registration.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified

title: Wildlife-damage compensation requires 12 documents for a payout capped near $65
description: Farmers in Nepal's Madhesh province alone reported 14,821 human-wildlife conflict cases in one year (mid-2024 to mid-2025) from nilgai, wild boar, deer, and elephants, but the government's relief guideline demands 12 types of supporting documents for a maximum payout of just Rs 10,000 (about $65), excludes crops on unregistered land, and covers only 16 specified animal species — leaving out common culprits like deer, peacocks and parrots. Many farmers report the travel cost to file a claim exceeds the compensation itself, so a large share of victims simply don't pursue relief.
severity_or_scale: 14,821 conflict cases in Madhesh in one year; compensation capped near Rs10,000 (~$65)

title: Forest fires increased roughly tenfold in a decade with almost no dedicated management budget
description: Nepal recorded more than 300 forest-fire incidents in just the first two months of 2025 alone, part of a roughly tenfold increase in wildfire frequency over the past decade driven by drier winters and reduced community-forest engagement as rural populations migrate away. The national disaster agency (NDRRMA) has gone without a dedicated forest-fire focal person for months at a time, and the Ministry of Forests allocated just NPR 22 million for wildfire management nationally — not enough to buy adequate portable water pumps and equipment.
severity_or_scale: wildfires up ~10x over a decade; 300+ incidents in the first 2 months of 2025; NPR 22 million total wildfire-management budget

title: Up to 7,000 rural girls are trafficked into Kathmandu as domestic servants annually
description: Reports estimate up to 7,000 girls from rural areas are brought into Kathmandu each year as domestic 'slaves,' where sexual abuse is common, and roughly 17,000 women and girls overall are trafficked annually from Nepal — including to India for sexual exploitation and to the Gulf and Malaysia under false promises of legitimate domestic or entertainment-sector work. There is no centralized, easily accessible verification tool families or the trafficked individuals themselves can use to check whether a job offer or destination household is legitimate before travel.
severity_or_scale: ~7,000 girls/year trafficked into Kathmandu for domestic work; ~17,000 women/girls trafficked annually overall

title: 3.5 million-plus people in the Terai are exposed to elevated groundwater arsenic
description: An estimated half a million people in Nepal's Terai are exposed to arsenic levels above 50 μg/L in their drinking water, and a further 3.5 million (31% of the region's population) face exposure between 10-50 μg/L, from naturally occurring geogenic arsenic leaching into shallow tube wells that serve as the primary water source. Iron-assisted biosand filters have proven effective in trials but haven't been distributed at the scale needed to protect the full affected population.
severity_or_scale: ~500,000 exposed above 50µg/L; 3.5 million (31% of Terai population) exposed to 10-50µg/L

title: Seasonal blood shortages leave hospitals dependent on army and police donors
description: Blood transfusion centers in Kathmandu, Dharan, Biratnagar and Chitwan face recurring shortages, worst during monsoon and the Dashain/Tihar festival season when voluntary donation drops just as demand continues, forcing hospitals to rely on Nepal Army, Police, and health-worker personnel to fill gaps. Some districts, like Bajura, lack a functional blood bank altogether, forcing patients' families to personally locate donors during emergencies, and blood-inventory management nationally is still largely manual with no real-time visibility across facilities.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified nationally; specific districts (e.g. Bajura) lack any functional blood bank

title: Rural patients face long transport delays reaching time-critical emergency care
description: In much of rural Nepal, road links to the nearest hospital may not exist, be seasonal, or be washed out, so patients with time-critical conditions (obstetric emergencies, heart attacks) face preventable-death risk directly linked to transport delay, per rural case studies. Helicopter evacuation exists as a backup but is prohibitively costly for most families, and organized ground ambulance services like Nepal Ambulance Service, launched in 2011, had only grown to 40 vehicles by 2020, concentrated around Kathmandu and adjoining hill areas rather than the most remote districts.
severity_or_scale: Nepal Ambulance Service fleet: 40 ambulances by 2020, concentrated near Kathmandu

title: None of Nepal's 18 outpatient mental-health facilities serve children or adolescents
description: Nepal has the second-highest youth suicide rate in South Asia, with an estimated 340,000 adolescents having attempted suicide and 470,000 having contemplated it, yet none of the country's 18 outpatient mental-health facilities provide services specifically for children or adolescents, and the country has only about 0.05 child/adolescent mental-health specialists per 100,000 people. Nepal spends under USD 1 per capita on mental health and has no dedicated mental health law, leaving a near-total service gap for the population segment showing the highest need.
severity_or_scale: 0 of 18 outpatient facilities serve children/adolescents; ~340,000 adolescents with suicide attempts; <USD1/capita mental-health spending

title: Nearly 5,000 teaching posts sit vacant as subject teachers avoid rural postings
description: Nepal faces a shortage projected to exceed 100,000 teachers within two to three years, with nearly 5,000 posts (grades 1-10) currently vacant because repeated advertisements for math, science and English positions fail to attract candidates willing to serve in remote areas. Schools cope by having lower-secondary teachers cover higher grades, widening the rural-urban learning gap — only 65% of rural children attend primary school versus 90% in urban areas, and many rural schools lack basic toilets or electricity.
severity_or_scale: ~5,000 current teacher vacancies; shortage projected to exceed 100,000 within 2-3 years; 65% rural vs 90% urban primary attendance

title: 6.7 million Nepalis lack citizenship certificates, blocking access to basic services
description: An estimated 6.7 million people in Nepal lack citizenship certificates, with children of single mothers, unmarried mothers, or fathers who deny paternity facing the steepest administrative barriers because Nepal's citizenship law still discriminates against women passing nationality to their children. Without certificates, affected children cannot access free primary education, enroll in university, open bank accounts, get passports, or access many healthcare and employment services — and Nepal has no formal statelessness-determination framework to resolve these cases.
severity_or_scale: ~6.7 million people lack Citizenship Certificates; 5,000+ children currently waiting

title: Elderly parents left behind by migrant children face isolation with no formal care system
description: As Nepal transitions toward an 'aging society' by 2028 (elderly share already up from 8.13% in 2011 to 10.21% in the 2021 census), many older parents whose children work abroad are left without a designated caregiver, and nearly two-thirds of older adults report depression, loneliness or anxiety despite living with extended family. No significant formal geriatric-care, home-visit-nursing, or senior-community-center infrastructure substitutes for the family caregiving that outmigration has removed.
severity_or_scale: elderly share of population rose from 8.13% (2011) to 10.21% (2021 census); ~2/3 of older adults report depression/loneliness/anxiety

title: Trekking porters die from exposure when agencies skip mandated gear and insurance
description: Despite guidelines requiring licensed trekking agencies to provide porters with life insurance, helicopter-rescue insurance, and adequate cold-weather gear, documented cases show porters dying of exposure specifically because an agency failed to provide proper equipment, with load limits (20-25kg) also inconsistently enforced. Because much of the trekking industry runs through informal or lightly-regulated local agencies, compliance depends heavily on individual operator ethics rather than systematic inspection.
severity_or_scale: documented fatal cases exist; no aggregate national count found

title: Everest generates roughly 12,000 kg of human waste a year with no scalable disposal system
description: Everest's spring climbing season alone generates about 21,500 kg of human waste as part of 75 tonnes of total waste, with roughly 12,000 kg of human waste produced yearly overall (80% of it in spring), and higher camps still have open latrines and melting-out buried waste with no oversight. New rules require climbers to carry waste down in bags, but authorities have only prepared enough bags for roughly 1,500 people (climbers, support staff, rescue teams combined) despite far larger seasonal footfall, and waste that does come down is dumped in unlined pits near Gorak Shep village, risking contamination.
severity_or_scale: ~12,000 kg human waste/year on Everest; bag supply prepared for only ~1,500 people

title: Three decades of Bagmati cleanup campaigns have failed to stop the river's pollution
description: A government committee dedicated specifically to cleaning the Bagmati River has operated for over 30 years without meeting its goal, as over 95% of Kathmandu Valley's wastewater is still discharged untreated directly into the river and its tributaries, compounded by encroachment and construction right up to the riverbanks. Volunteer cleanup campaigns have removed tens of thousands of tons of waste over the years, but frequent disruptions to regular municipal trash collection mean dumping continues faster than volunteers or authorities can keep up.
severity_or_scale: 30+ years of failed cleanup campaign; >95% of wastewater discharged untreated; 20,000 tons of waste extracted from the Bagmati in five years of one campaign

title: Informal-sector workers remain largely excluded from Nepal's Social Security Fund
description: Roughly 84.6% of Nepal's employed population works informally, yet the country's contributory Social Security Fund has historically covered mainly formal-sector and migrant workers; while policy now nominally extends the SSF to informal and self-employed workers, actual enrollment, awareness, and implementation among this group remain very limited. This leaves the vast majority of Nepal's workforce without medical, maternity, disability, or old-age protection tied to their employment.
severity_or_scale: 84.6% of employed population in informal employment; ~2.7 million private-sector workers enrolled in SSF as of one recent count, mostly formal-sector

title: Chhaupadi menstrual exile continues to kill women despite a 2018 criminal ban
description: Even after Nepal criminalized chhaupadi (banishing menstruating women and girls to outdoor huts) in August 2018 with fines and jail terms, women continue to die from exposure, smoke inhalation, and snake or animal bites in far-western and mid-western districts, and enforcement has been so weak that the first arrest over a chhaupadi-related death only came in December 2019. Even where huts have been physically demolished, families often simply isolate women in a different, equally under-resourced space in or near the home, meaning the underlying practice persists in a less visible form.
severity_or_scale: documented recurring annual deaths in the far-west (multiple named cases 2016-2019); enforcement remains weak years after 2018 criminalization

title: Stalled Cannabis Cultivation Act blocks a legal hemp and medical-cannabis export industry
description: A draft Cannabis Cultivation, Regulation and Management Act that would formalize medical cannabis and industrial hemp production has sat without progress for more than two years, even though hemp fiber and seed are already legal (only the flower remains banned under the 1976 Narcotic Drugs Control Act) and researchers estimate Nepal could produce millions of tonnes of hemp-based solid fuel, fiber, and biodiesel annually. Activists went on hunger strike in 2024 demanding even a hearing on a four-year-old legalization petition, illustrating how far behind other cannabis-legalizing markets Nepal's regulatory process lags on a crop it can already grow well agronomically.
severity_or_scale: bill stalled 2+ years; underlying legalization petition pending 4+ years

title: Kathmandu's roughly 19,000 stray dogs create recurring bite/rabies risk with only partial sterilization coverage
description: Kathmandu's stray dog population is estimated at 19,000-24,000, and while the Metropolitan City has adopted a Catch-Neuter-Vaccinate-Release program (targeting 10,000+ sterilizations in a recent budget year) instead of culling, coverage remains partial relative to the total population and reproduction rate, so bite incidents and rabies risk persist. Smaller municipalities without KMC's budget or NGO partnerships have far less capacity to run even a partial CNVR program.
severity_or_scale: ~19,000-24,000 stray dogs in Kathmandu; ~10,000 sterilizations budgeted in one recent year against that base population

title: Recruitment agencies deceive most migrant workers about actual contract terms
description: A survey found almost two-thirds of Nepali migrant workers to Malaysia and the Gulf paid excessive, illegal recruitment fees despite laws limiting such charges, and Amnesty International found 90% of surveyed migrants had been deceived by recruitment agencies about their actual contract terms. Because visas are typically tied to a single employer, workers who discover the deception after arrival risk becoming undocumented if they leave, trapping them in exploitative conditions rather than able to seek redress.
severity_or_scale: ~90% of surveyed migrants deceived about contract terms; ~2/3 paid illegal recruitment fees

title: Education consultancies exploit study-abroad dreams to run undisclosed foreign-employment rackets
description: Nepal Police have arrested dozens of education-consultancy operators (69 in one Kathmandu Valley crackdown alone) for allegedly using student-visa applications as cover to funnel people into foreign employment, or for charging Rs 700,000-1,200,000 per client while supplying forged documents; a Dubai-linked case alone left at least 65 Nepali students cheated, with some now living as undocumented residents after losing visas due to the fraud. Weak licensing oversight lets unlicensed operators offer counseling, test-prep, and visa services without verified credentials.
severity_or_scale: 69 consultancy operators investigated in one crackdown; 65+ students cheated in one documented Dubai case

title: No structured skills-recognition pathway exists for returning migrant workers
description: Nepali workers returning after years of Gulf or Malaysia construction, hospitality, or manufacturing employment generally have no formal mechanism to have their overseas-acquired skills certified or recognized by Nepali employers or CTEVT-equivalent bodies, so returnees often re-enter the domestic labor market at entry-level despite years of relevant experience. This wastes accumulated human capital exactly when Nepal needs skilled labor for infrastructure and industrial projects.
severity_or_scale: impact not quantified
